stories.title: Parliament takes up a bill to expand the Supreme Court from 33 to 37 judges, replacing a May ordinance
key_points: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026** would raise the court's sanctioned strength (excluding the Chief Justice) from **33 to 37 judges**.
It **replaces an ordinance** the government had already issued on **May 16, 2026** to make the change immediately, before Parliament could vote on it.
The **Lok Sabha took up the bill on Thursday**, July 30, as part of the ongoing Monsoon Session.
Opposition MPs **Sougata Ray, N.K. Premachandran, and Dean Kuriakose** moved a statutory resolution seeking to **disapprove of the original ordinance**.
The government says more judges will help the Supreme Court **clear its backlog and deliver faster justice**.
stories.background: India's Supreme Court has for years struggled with a **massive case backlog** — tens of thousands of pending cases — partly because its sanctioned judge strength hasn't kept pace with the volume of appeals reaching it. When Parliament isn't in session, the government can issue an **ordinance** — a temporary law with the force of legislation — to act quickly, but ordinances **must be replaced by a proper law within six months** or they lapse. The government used this route in May 2026 to expand the court immediately, and is now asking Parliament to formally convert that ordinance into permanent law.
stories.what_happened: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026**, which raises the court's judge count from **33 to 37** (not counting the Chief Justice of India), was introduced in the Lok Sabha on **July 20** by Law Minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal**, and the House took it up for consideration and passage on **Thursday, July 30**. The bill formally replaces an **ordinance the government had already issued on May 16, 2026** to expand the court before Parliament reconvened. Opposition MPs Sougata Ray, N.K. Premachandran, and Dean Kuriakose used a **statutory resolution** — a parliamentary tool to formally object to a government ordinance — to challenge the original move, arguing it should have gone through Parliament first rather than being enacted by executive order.
stories.why_it_matters: More judges could meaningfully speed up how fast the Supreme Court hears and resolves cases, directly affecting how quickly ordinary litigants — from criminal appeals to constitutional disputes — get resolutions. The ordinance-then-ratify process also raises a recurring question about how much lawmaking should happen by executive order versus full parliamentary debate.
stories.ripple_effects: If passed, the Chief Justice and the Collegium (the panel of senior judges that recommends new judicial appointments in India) will need to identify and process four additional appointments, a process that itself typically takes months. It could also renew debate over judicial appointment processes more broadly.
stories.why_now: The bill is up now because ordinances have a six-month legal shelf life — the May 16 ordinance needs Parliament's formal ratification well before that window closes, and the Monsoon Session is the government's opportunity to do it.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the bill's final vote count and whether the Rajya Sabha takes it up next, plus how quickly the Collegium moves to recommend the four new judges.

key_terms.definition: A law issued directly by India's President (on the government's advice) when Parliament isn't in session — it has the force of law but must be approved by Parliament within six months or it lapses.
The system by which India's most senior Supreme Court judges, led by the Chief Justice, recommend judges for appointment and transfer — rather than the executive branch selecting them directly.

stories.the_lesson: Adding capacity (more judges, more staff, more courts) is often a simpler fix for institutional backlogs than procedural reform — but it still has to survive the political process of turning a stopgap executive order into a lasting law.

stories.title: Rajya Sabha passes the anti-paper-leak bill amid an opposition walkout over the NEET leaks and Delhi crackdown
key_points: The **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026** cleared the **Rajya Sabha on Thursday**, a day after passing the Lok Sabha.
It adds **stricter penalties, time-bound investigations, and Special Fast Track Courts** to punish cheating and paper leaks in government exams.
**Opposition MPs, led by Mallikarjun Kharge, walked out** before the vote, criticizing the government's handling of the **NEET paper leak and a July 20 Delhi protest crackdown**.
A **Special Task Force** will now be required to complete paper-leak investigations within **2–3 months**, per the government.
The bill now goes to the **President for assent** before it becomes law.
stories.background: Paper leaks — cases where question papers for major government and entrance exams (like **NEET**, the medical-college entrance test) are stolen and sold or shared before the exam — have repeatedly disrupted Indian recruitment and admissions in recent years, forcing exam cancellations and derailing the futures of lakhs of students. India already passed a **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act** in 2024 to criminalize this, but enforcement gaps remained, particularly around investigation timelines and specialized courts. This amendment tightens that framework. It comes against the backdrop of ongoing anger over the recent NEET leak and a controversial **July 20 police crackdown on student protesters in Delhi**, which the opposition has been demanding answers on.
stories.what_happened: The **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026** passed the **Rajya Sabha** (India's upper house of Parliament) on Thursday, July 30, a day after clearing the **Lok Sabha** (the lower house) on Wednesday. The bill strengthens India's 2024 anti-cheating law by adding **stricter penalties, mandatory time-bound investigations, and dedicated Special Fast Track Courts** to handle paper-leak and exam-fraud cases. During the debate, **Congress MP Mallikarjun Kharge** led criticism of the government over the recent **NEET paper leak** and its handling of the **July 20 crackdown on student protesters** in Delhi. Opposition MPs **walked out of the Rajya Sabha before the final vote**. Union Minister **Jitendra Singh** said the newly empowered Special Task Force will be required to complete its investigations within **2–3 months**. The bill now heads to the **President of India** for formal assent before becoming law.
stories.why_it_matters: Paper leaks have derailed recruitment and college-admission exams for millions of Indian students in recent years, so faster, tougher enforcement directly affects how trustworthy India's exam system is. The opposition walkout also shows the leak issue remains politically live, tied to broader anger over how the government has handled recent protests.
stories.ripple_effects: Students and coaching institutes will watch closely for how quickly the new Fast Track Courts start functioning, since past cases have dragged on for years. The political fight over the July 20 Delhi crackdown is likely to continue in Parliament regardless of this bill's passage, keeping pressure on Home Minister Amit Shah.
stories.why_now: The bill was already moving through Parliament's ongoing **Monsoon Session**, and its passage this week comes directly on the heels of a fresh NEET-related leak controversy that gave the opposition a specific case to point to during debate.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the President's assent (a formality expected soon) and whether the first Special Fast Track Court cases are filed within the government's promised 2–3 month window.

key_terms.definition: India's National Eligibility cum Entrance Test — the single national exam required to get into medical colleges, taken by over 2 million students a year.
A court set up to resolve specific categories of cases faster than the regular judicial process, usually with dedicated judges and shorter timelines.

stories.the_lesson: Passing a law is often the easier half of fixing a systemic problem — the harder half is building the fast, well-resourced enforcement machinery (investigators, courts) that makes the law actually bite.

stories.title: Indo-MIM shares surge 45% on debut after one of 2026's most oversubscribed IPOs
key_points: Indo-MIM's stock **listed at a 44–45% premium** over its ₹485 issue price on both NSE and BSE.
The **₹3,810 crore IPO was subscribed 72.37 times** overall, with institutional investors bidding for **over 204 times** their allotted portion.
Indo-MIM is a **Bengaluru-based precision-parts maker** using metal injection moulding (MIM) — components used in cars, defence gear, and medical devices, sold to **45+ countries**.
Elsewhere on Dalal Street, **Waaree Energies fell over 6%** the same day as investors scrutinised its margins after Q1 results.
Two smaller IPOs, **Lohia Corp and Xtranet Technologies**, also listed today with modest single-digit premiums.
stories.background: An IPO (Initial Public Offering) is when a private company first sells shares to the public and starts trading on a stock exchange. How eagerly investors 'subscribe' (bid for shares) before listing, and how much the stock jumps on its first trading day versus its issue price, are widely watched signals of investor appetite — both for that specific company and for the broader IPO market. Indo-MIM, founded in 1996, makes small, complex metal components — the kind used inside cars, medical devices, and defence equipment — using a specialised manufacturing process called metal injection moulding (MIM), and supplies customers in more than 45 countries.
stories.what_happened: Indo-MIM Limited debuted on Indian stock exchanges on July 30, 2026, listing at **₹700 on the NSE** (a 44.33% premium over its ₹485 issue price) and **₹703 on the BSE** (a 44.95% premium). The company's **₹3,810.31 crore IPO** — comprising a ₹499.10 crore fresh share issue plus a ₹3,311.21 crore offer-for-sale by existing shareholders — was open for bidding from July 23–27 and ended up **72.37 times oversubscribed**, with the institutional (QIB) portion alone subscribed **over 204 times**. It was one of three IPOs listing on Indian exchanges the same day; **Lohia Corp** listed at a 7.09% premium and **Xtranet Technologies** also gained modestly, both far more muted than Indo-MIM's debut. On the same trading day, **Waaree Energies**, a large solar-equipment maker, fell more than 6% as investors focused on margin pressure in its latest quarterly results — illustrating that Indian markets are simultaneously rewarding a strong new listing and punishing profit concerns at an established company.
stories.why_it_matters: A 72x-oversubscribed, 45%-premium listing signals strong investor confidence in India's IPO market and in niche manufacturing exporters specifically — relevant as India tries to position itself as a 'China Plus One' manufacturing alternative for global supply chains. It's also a real-money test of risk appetite at a moment when the broader economy is showing some strain.
stories.ripple_effects: A hot IPO debut like this can encourage more private manufacturing companies to go public in the coming months, and gives early institutional investors an immediate paper profit. It also draws retail investor attention and money toward IPOs generally, which can pull some liquidity away from existing listed stocks in the near term.
stories.why_now: The listing happened today, July 30, 2026, as the culmination of a subscription window that closed July 27.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether Indo-MIM holds onto its listing-day gains over the next few sessions, which is often a better signal of durable investor confidence than the debut pop itself.

key_terms.definition: When investors bid for more shares than a company is actually offering in its IPO — e.g., '72 times oversubscribed' means demand was 72x the shares available.
Part of an IPO where existing shareholders — not the company — sell their own shares to the public, so that portion of the proceeds goes to them, not the company.

stories.the_lesson: A red-hot IPO debut and a rough day for an established stock can happen on the same market, the same day — headline market sentiment often hides very different stories playing out company by company.
stories.market_link: Direct: NSE/BSE listing of Indo-MIM; sentiment read-through for India's broader 2026 IPO pipeline.

stories.title: India's economy flashes warning signs: trade gap widens, growth slows to a 4-year low, monsoon stays patchy
key_points: India's **merchandise trade deficit widened to $30.43 billion** in June, up from $28.21bn in May, as imports **surged 31%** while exports rose 15.5%.
**Economic activity growth slowed to its weakest pace in more than four years** in July, per Bloomberg's tracking, as Middle East tensions and tariffs raised costs.
**US tariffs** aimed at curbing India's purchases of discounted Russian oil pushed up the cost of imported energy.
The **monsoon rainfall deficit**, which had spiked to 40% earlier in July, has since narrowed to around **15%** after a burst of late-July rain — still leaving farm output at risk.
**RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra** flagged the Iran war and a weak monsoon as the two biggest near-term risks to India's growth.
stories.background: India has spent much of 2026 dealing with the economic fallout of the wider Middle East conflict: higher oil import costs, disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz (the narrow waterway that much of the world's oil passes through), and new US tariffs targeting countries — including India — that kept buying discounted Russian crude oil despite Western sanctions. At the same time, India relies heavily on a good **monsoon season** (June–September) both to water crops directly and to recharge reservoirs that irrigate farms later in the year; a weak monsoon quickly shows up as higher food inflation and slower rural spending.
stories.what_happened: A Bloomberg roundup published July 29, 2026 describes India's economy as sending 'mixed signals' as businesses navigate simultaneous war-related and trade-related shocks. On the trade front, India's **exports grew 15.5% to $40.41 billion** in June — a genuinely strong number, led by electronics and engineering goods — but **imports jumped 31% to a record $70.84 billion**, mainly due to costlier energy imports, widening the trade deficit to **$30.43 billion**, well above the roughly $26.5 billion economists had expected. Separately, broader economic activity tracking showed India's growth slowing to its **weakest pace in more than four years** in July. On the weather side, the monsoon has been volatile: a strong start cut the seasonal rainfall deficit from 40% to 14%, a dry spell pushed it back up to 24%, and a fresh burst of rain between July 21–24 brought it back down to roughly **15%** — still a shortfall, with knock-on risk to crop yields and rural incomes. RBI Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** has publicly named the Iran war and the weak monsoon as the two key risks clouding the outlook.
stories.why_it_matters: India has been marketed globally as 'the world's fastest-growing major economy' — this data shows that story colliding with real headwinds: costlier imported energy, US trade pressure over Russian oil purchases, and unreliable rain. How the government and RBI respond will shape jobs, food prices, and the rupee's strength for ordinary Indians in the coming months.
stories.ripple_effects: A wider trade deficit and slower growth typically pressure the **rupee** to weaken, which then makes imported goods — including that same oil — even more expensive, a vicious cycle. A patchy monsoon can push up prices of vegetables and pulses at the local market within weeks. Investors may also grow more cautious on India-linked assets if the 'mixed signals' narrative persists into the next data releases.
stories.why_now: This is surfacing today because Bloomberg's July 29 analysis pulled together the most recent set of releases — June trade data, July activity tracking, and evolving monsoon numbers — into a single, sharper 'warning signs' narrative.
stories.watch_next: Watch India's Q1 FY27 GDP print and the next monthly trade data release for whether the slowdown deepens or the strong export growth offsets it.

key_terms.definition: A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that a large share of the world's traded oil passes through — disruptions there raise oil prices worldwide.
The gap when a country imports more, in dollar value, than it exports — a widening deficit generally pressures the currency and drains foreign reserves.

stories.the_lesson: Fast headline growth and underlying stress can coexist — a country can be the 'fastest-growing major economy' in aggregate while specific pressures like energy costs, trade friction, and weather quietly erode the picture underneath.
stories.market_link: Pressure on the rupee (USD/INR), import-heavy sectors, and RBI rate-decision expectations.

stories.title: IMD issues a red alert as a 'deep depression' dumps extreme rain on Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh
key_points: India's weather office (**IMD**) issued a **red alert** — its highest warning level — for **Odisha and Chhattisgarh** as a deep depression crosses the region.
Isolated pockets could see **over 204.5mm of rain** in a single day, enough to trigger flash floods and landslides.
The depression is moving **westward across Chhattisgarh** and is expected to weaken gradually over the next 24-48 hours.
The IMD warns that heavy to very heavy rain will hit **more than 20 states**, including Madhya Pradesh, Vidarbha (Maharashtra), Jharkhand and North India, over the coming week.
This adds to an already active monsoon that has caused flooding in Assam and landslides in Himachal Pradesh in recent days.
stories.background: A 'deep depression' is one step below a cyclone on India's monsoon storm-intensity scale — a large, organized low-pressure system that draws in huge amounts of moisture and dumps it as intense rain over whatever land it crosses. Central and eastern India — states like Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh — regularly see several of these systems form over the Bay of Bengal each monsoon season, and they're a major driver of both the farm-friendly rain India's economy depends on and the flash floods that displace people every year.
stories.what_happened: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** issued a **red alert for Odisha and Chhattisgarh**, warning that a deep depression crossing the region could dump **isolated extremely heavy rainfall exceeding 204.5mm in a day** — enough to cause flash floods, waterlogging and landslides in vulnerable areas. As of the IMD's Thursday bulletin, the system was centered over **west-central Chhattisgarh and adjoining Vidarbha and southeast Madhya Pradesh**, moving westward and expected to weaken into a depression and then a low-pressure area over the next day or so. The IMD separately warned that torrential rain and thunderstorms will continue for the **next seven days across more than 20 states**, including Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand and swathes of North India, as this system interacts with a second weather pattern. The alert comes on top of an already damaging monsoon season, with flood tolls rising in Assam and landslides blocking 150+ roads in Himachal Pradesh in recent days.
stories.why_it_matters: A red alert is the IMD's signal to state governments to activate disaster response — evacuate flood-prone areas, halt non-essential travel, and pre-position rescue teams — because the risk to life is judged serious, not just inconvenient.
stories.ripple_effects: Farmers in the affected states could see short-term crop damage from waterlogging even as the same rain replenishes reservoirs and groundwater for the rest of the year. Road and rail disruption in central India can ripple into freight delays. Local governments and disaster-response teams typically surge personnel into red-alert districts ahead of the worst rainfall.
stories.why_now: The depression formed over the Bay of Bengal and made landfall, and is now tracking directly over Odisha and Chhattisgarh at peak intensity, which is why the alert was escalated to red today.
stories.watch_next: Whether the system weakens on schedule over the next 24-48 hours as forecast, or intensifies further before crossing into Madhya Pradesh.

key_terms.definition: A large monsoon storm system one step below a cyclone in intensity, capable of dumping extremely heavy rain over a wide area as it crosses land.

stories.the_lesson: India's monsoon is both the country's most important economic event and one of its biggest recurring disaster risks — the same rain system a farmer needs can be the one that floods a neighboring district, which is why forecasts are issued district-by-district, not just state-by-state.

stories.title: Lok Sabha extends the 'One Nation, One Election' committee's deadline to the Monsoon Session's final week
key_points: The Lok Sabha (India's lower house of Parliament) approved another extension for the **41-member Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC)** studying the 'One Nation, One Election' bills.
The JPC is examining the **Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill**, which would let Lok Sabha, state assembly and eventually local body elections happen **on a single common schedule**.
The extension, moved by JPC chairman **P.P. Chaudhary**, was passed by a **voice vote** — no formal division was called.
The committee's new deadline is the **first day of the last week of the 2026 Monsoon Session**, but it may seek yet another extension given the scale of the consultations.
The JPC is meant to submit a **final report during the Winter Session** after consulting stakeholders across the country.
stories.background: 'One Nation, One Election' is a long-standing proposal, championed by the Modi government, to synchronize India's staggered election calendar — where different states currently vote for their assemblies at different times — into a single nationwide cycle held alongside Lok Sabha elections. Supporters argue it would cut the cost and administrative strain of near-constant campaigning; critics argue it could weaken state-level accountability. The **Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill**, which would enable the change, was referred to a specially formed **41-member Joint Parliamentary Committee** for detailed scrutiny because it touches the structure of India's federal democracy.
stories.what_happened: The Lok Sabha voted to **extend the JPC's working deadline again**, pushing it to the **first day of the last week of the ongoing 2026 Monsoon Session**. JPC chairman **P.P. Chaudhary** moved the extension resolution, and the House passed it on a **voice vote** rather than a recorded division. The extension gives the committee more time to continue consulting stakeholders — political parties, state governments, legal experts and the public — across the country before finalizing its position. Sources close to the committee suggest it may seek a **further extension** given how complex and contested the underlying constitutional questions are, meaning a final report is now expected only in the **Winter Session** of Parliament.
stories.why_it_matters: This bill would change the basic rhythm of Indian democracy — how often, and on what calendar, roughly a billion voters go to the polls. A delay signals the government is not rushing a constitutionally sensitive change through without broader buy-in, but it also means the political and logistical uncertainty around India's election calendar continues.
stories.ripple_effects: State governments and opposition parties, many of whom see 'One Nation, One Election' as diluting state-level politics, get more time to organize opposition or negotiate changes. Election Commission planning for the next multi-state election cycle stays in limbo until the JPC reports. Political positioning on this issue will likely resurface each time Parliament's sessions approach a deadline.
stories.why_now: The extension was needed because the JPC's previous deadline fell within the current Monsoon Session, and the committee said its stakeholder consultations are not yet complete.
stories.watch_next: Whether the JPC meets its new end-of-Monsoon-Session deadline or requests another extension into the Winter Session, as sources suggest is likely.

key_terms.definition: A committee made up of members from both houses of India's Parliament, formed to give a bill detailed, cross-party scrutiny before it comes back for a full vote.

stories.the_lesson: Major constitutional changes in a democracy usually move slowly on purpose — repeated extensions for consultation are a feature of getting buy-in, not just bureaucratic delay.

stories.title: Supreme Court won't ban pellet guns outright, but orders Delhi to treat protesters injured by them
key_points: The Supreme Court said pellet guns **can't be banned outright** as long as an existing government advisory allows their use for crowd control in exceptional situations.
The Court directed the **Delhi government to ensure proper medical treatment** for people allegedly injured by pellet guns during recent student protests.
The case stems from the **July 20 'Chalo Sansad' march**, where student protesters and police clashed near Jantar Mantar over an alleged **NEET-UG paper leak**.
Petitioners included a **former Central Information Commissioner and retired IPS officer**, plus two people who say they were injured by pellets.
The Court left the door open for **case-by-case scrutiny** of specific alleged misuse, even while declining a blanket ban.
stories.background: Pellet guns fire clusters of small metal or rubber pellets and are officially classed as a 'less lethal' crowd-control weapon, but they've caused serious injuries — including blindings — in India before, most notably during unrest in Jammu & Kashmir. On **July 20, 2026**, a student march called 'Chalo Sansad' (loosely, 'let's go to Parliament') turned violent near Jantar Mantar in Delhi, with protesters angry over an alleged leak of the NEET-UG medical entrance exam paper; clashes broke out between demonstrators and security personnel, leaving people on both sides injured. That clash has already become a political flashpoint this week, with opposition leader Rahul Gandhi accusing Home Minister Amit Shah of ordering students to be shot at, a charge the government denies — so this Supreme Court case is the judicial track of a story that's also playing out as a political fight in Parliament.
stories.what_happened: A Supreme Court bench, with Justice Bagchi delivering key remarks, held on Thursday that pellet guns cannot be subject to a **blanket prohibition** because an existing police advisory permits their use in exceptional crowd-control circumstances, and that advisory itself hasn't been legally challenged. The Court said allegations of specific misuse in individual incidents can still be examined **case by case**. At the same time, it **directed the Delhi government to ensure proper medical treatment** for people injured, allegedly by pellet guns, during the protests. It also sought the **Centre's Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)** on pellet gun use and issued formal notice on the broader petition. The plea was brought by **Yashovardhan Azad**, a former Central Information Commissioner and retired IPS officer, along with two individuals who say they were injured, seeking a complete ban on metallic pellet guns for law-and-order use. The underlying incident was the violence during the July 20 Chalo Sansad march over the alleged NEET-UG paper leak.
stories.why_it_matters: This sets a real legal boundary on how far courts will go in restricting a widely-used (if controversial) crowd-control tool, while still holding the government accountable for the human cost of using it — a middle path that neither fully satisfies police-reform advocates nor removes the tool from law enforcement's hands.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect this case to keep surfacing procedurally (the Centre must now produce its SOP), and for it to be cited both by the government (as vindication that pellet guns remain lawful) and by petitioners (as a partial win, since injured protesters now have a court-ordered right to treatment). It also keeps judicial and political scrutiny on the events of July 20 alive even as the political blame-game over the same protests continues separately in Parliament.
stories.why_now: The petition was filed in the immediate aftermath of the July 20 protest violence, and the Court took it up this week as the broader political row over the same incident escalated in the Rajya Sabha.
stories.watch_next: The Centre's formal SOP submission on pellet gun use, and any case-specific misuse complaints the Court agrees to examine individually.

key_terms.definition: A government's official, written rulebook for how a specific action — here, pellet gun use — is supposed to be carried out.

stories.the_lesson: Courts often avoid blanket bans on contested tools and instead set narrower guardrails — accountability for misuse and a right to treatment — which can look like a split decision but actually reflects how much courts weigh existing government policy before overriding it.

stories.title: Sensex jumps 889 points and Nifty IT surges as Infosys results and the Fed's rate hold lift sentiment
key_points: The Sensex climbed **888.68 points (1.16%)** to close at **77,654.60**; the Nifty 50 rose **264.85 points (1.10%)** to **24,250.20**.
**Nifty IT jumped over 2.3%** in a single session and is up **nearly 16% for the month of July** — one of the sector's sharpest rallies in years.
**Infosys** led the charge after strong Q1 FY27 results: consolidated net profit rose **9% year-on-year to ₹6,921 crore**, revenue rose **8% to ₹42,279 crore**.
A weaker **rupee-driven currency tailwind** and **FII short-covering** (foreign investors closing bearish bets) added extra fuel to the rally.
The rally came right after the **US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady**, which investors read as reducing near-term global risk.
stories.background: India's stock market runs on two headline indices: the **Sensex** (30 large companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange) and the **Nifty 50** (50 large companies on the National Stock Exchange) — both are 'scoreboards' for how big Indian companies are doing as a group. IT services (companies like Infosys, TCS, and Wipro that sell software and outsourcing services mostly to Western clients) is one of India's largest and most export-driven sectors, so it's highly sensitive to the **rupee's exchange rate** (a weaker rupee means the dollar revenue these firms earn abroad converts into more rupees at home) and to US economic health, since America is their biggest client base. The sector had been in a slump for much of 2026 after a slower spending environment among Western clients, hitting a 52-week low as recently as **July 1**.
stories.what_happened: The **BSE Sensex gained 888.68 points, or 1.16%,** to close at **77,654.60** on Wednesday, July 29, while the **Nifty 50 advanced 264.85 points, or 1.10%,** to **24,250.20**. The rally was led by technology stocks: the **Nifty IT index jumped roughly 2.3% in the session** and has now climbed **nearly 16% in July alone**, recovering more than 21% from its 52-week low touched on July 1. **Infosys** was the standout, gaining after it posted **9% year-on-year growth in consolidated net profit to ₹6,921 crore** and **8% revenue growth to ₹42,279 crore** for the quarter ended June, with investors also cheering its forward earnings commentary. Banking stocks also firmed, with the Bank Nifty index up 0.79% to 57,205.90. Analysts pointed to a combination of factors: a stronger rupee, foreign institutional investors covering short positions (buying back stock they had bet against), and calmer global sentiment after the **US Federal Reserve's decision a day earlier to hold interest rates steady** rather than signal further tightening.
stories.why_it_matters: This rally matters beyond one trading day because it shows India's IT sector — a huge employer and export earner — potentially turning a corner after a rough stretch, and because it shows how directly global central-bank decisions (in this case the Fed's) ripple into Indian portfolios within 24 hours.
stories.ripple_effects: A sustained IT rally would help the rupee (more dollar export earnings), support employment in India's biggest white-collar export industry, and could pull in more foreign investment if the trend holds through the rest of earnings season (TCS, Wipro, HCLTech results still to come). If global rate-cut hopes fade, though, this kind of rally can reverse quickly.
stories.why_now: Q1 FY27 earnings season for India's biggest IT firms is underway, and Infosys's better-than-expected numbers landed the same week global markets got reassurance from the Fed's decision to hold rates — a rare alignment of a strong local catalyst and a calmer global backdrop.
stories.watch_next: TCS, Wipro, and HCLTech's remaining Q1 FY27 results in the coming days, to see if Infosys's strength is sector-wide or company-specific.

key_terms.definition: When foreign investors who had bet a stock or index would fall are forced to buy it back to close those bets, which itself pushes the price up further.

stories.the_lesson: A single earnings beat from a sector bellwether (like Infosys for Indian IT) can trigger a rally across an entire sector, because investors read one company's results as a signal about the health of all its peers.
stories.market_link: Nifty IT names (Infosys, TCS, Coforge, LTIMindtree) and the broader Nifty 50/Sensex indices are the direct plays here; a stronger rupee is the other side of the same trade.

stories.title: RBI's July bulletin shows India's economy holding steady on stronger FDI, FPI, and a surprise current-account surplus
key_points: RBI's July bulletin says **strong industrial activity and exports** are keeping India's economy on a steady path
**Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** in April–May 2026 was higher than the same period last year
**Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI)** turned positive in June and stayed positive through July
India posted a **$4.7 billion current-account surplus** in April, reversing a **$4.8 billion deficit** a year earlier
RBI temporarily lifted the interest-rate ceiling on 3–5 year **NRI foreign-currency deposits** through September 30
stories.background: India's economy has been sending mixed signals lately — a weak monsoon and global trade shocks (including new US tariffs) have weighed on some indicators even as underlying growth held up. The Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank, publishes a monthly bulletin assessing the state of the economy, and its July edition paints a notably more resilient picture: rising investment inflows and a swing back to a current-account surplus, a sign the country is earning more from trade, services, and remittances than it's spending abroad.
stories.what_happened: The RBI's July 2026 bulletin reported that **strong industrial activity, a healthy services sector, rising exports, and improving foreign investment** have kept India's economy resilient even as many other countries face headwinds. **FDI in April–May 2026 came in higher** than the same two months last year, and **FPI — money foreign investors put into Indian stocks and bonds — turned positive in June and stayed positive in July**, reversing earlier outflows. India's **current account recorded a $4.7 billion surplus in April 2026**, a sharp reversal from a $4.8 billion deficit a year earlier, driven by **net services exports strengthening to $18.6 billion** and **remittances surging to $16 billion** from $9.4 billion. Separately, the RBI **temporarily removed the interest-rate ceiling on foreign-currency (FCNR-B) deposits** with 3–5 year tenors, effective through September 30, giving banks more room to attract NRI deposits.
stories.why_it_matters: These numbers matter because they're the clearest sign yet that foreign investors are coming back to India after a period of caution, and that India is earning a genuine surplus on its trade and services with the rest of the world rather than relying on borrowing to cover a deficit.
stories.ripple_effects: A stronger current account and rising FPI typically support the rupee and give the RBI more room on interest-rate policy. It could also make it easier for Indian companies and banks to raise foreign capital, and gives the government a stronger hand heading into ongoing India-US trade negotiations.
stories.why_now: The RBI publishes this bulletin monthly, and July's edition is the first to fully capture the June–July rebound in foreign portfolio flows after a rockier first half of the year.
stories.watch_next: Whether FPI inflows and the current-account surplus hold up through the next quarter, especially once new US tariffs on Indian goods take fuller effect.

key_terms.definition: A country's overall balance of trade, services, and income with the rest of the world; a surplus means it earns more from abroad than it spends, a deficit means the opposite.

stories.the_lesson: Headline growth numbers can look 'mixed' while the underlying balance of payments quietly improves — it pays to look past the loudest indicator (like a weak monsoon) to the ones that actually move a currency and interest rates.
stories.market_link: A stronger current account and returning FPI flows are typically supportive of the Indian rupee and Indian equities.

stories.title: Rahul Gandhi and Congress escalate pressure on Amit Shah in Rajya Sabha over student 'lathi-charge' claim
key_points: Congress's **Pramod Tiwari** told the Rajya Sabha students were **'lathi-charged, pellet fire used'** and Shah must answer
Rahul Gandhi asked why **Amit Shah is 'so scared' of Parliament**, saying his absence 'reeks of guilt'
Tiwari invoked **Article 75** of the Constitution to argue Shah is directly accountable to the House
The clash came as the **Public Examinations Amendment Bill** was tabled in the Rajya Sabha a day after Lok Sabha passage
It's the same **July 20 student-protest** episode Gandhi raised in the Lok Sabha two days ago
stories.background: On Wednesday, Rahul Gandhi told the Lok Sabha that Home Minister Amit Shah had personally ordered police to fire on students protesting near Jantar Mantar on July 20, calling it a 'shooting' of students and saying police put 'pellets into the blood' of protesters. The government flatly denied it, with ministers saying only tear gas was used and demanding Gandhi apologize for what they called a breach of parliamentary privilege. The clash overshadowed passage of the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, itself a response to this year's NEET-UG paper-leak protests.
stories.what_happened: The confrontation moved to the **Rajya Sabha** on Thursday as the same Public Examinations Amendment Bill was tabled there a day after clearing the Lok Sabha. Congress's deputy leader in the Rajya Sabha, **Pramod Tiwari**, told the House that **'students were lathi-charged, pellet fire used'** during the July 20 protest and that Home Minister Amit Shah, as the constitutionally accountable minister under **Article 75**, must personally answer for it. Separately, Rahul Gandhi told reporters he personally witnessed Shah **'calling the police'** during the protest, and asked **'Why is Amit Shah so scared of coming to Parliament?'**, saying his absence from the debate 'reeks of guilt.' The government has not issued a fresh on-record rebuttal to Thursday's remarks beyond its Wednesday denial that any shots were fired.
stories.why_it_matters: This has escalated from a one-day Lok Sabha clash into a sustained, cross-House political confrontation over how police handled a student protest — with the Home Minister's personal accountability now the central question, not just what happened on July 20.
stories.ripple_effects: A prolonged stand-off could disrupt the rest of the Monsoon Session's legislative agenda, including the SC Judges Bill also listed for today. It also keeps the NEET-UG paper-leak protest movement in the news cycle and raises the political cost for the government the longer Shah stays out of the debate.
stories.why_now: The Public Examinations Bill's move to the Rajya Sabha today gave the opposition a fresh procedural opening to revive Wednesday's unresolved clash over the same underlying protest.
stories.watch_next: Whether Amit Shah personally responds in Parliament, and whether the stand-off delays the Rajya Sabha's own vote on the exam-leak bill.

key_terms.definition: The constitutional provision that makes India's Council of Ministers, including the Home Minister, collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (and by convention, answerable to Parliament generally).

stories.the_lesson: In parliamentary systems, a minister's silence in the House can become as politically costly as the original incident — accountability isn't just about what happened, but whether you show up to answer for it.

thread.previously: We reported that Gandhi accused Shah of ordering police to fire on students and use pellets during a July 20 protest, which the government denied, saying only tear gas was used, and demanded Gandhi apologise for a breach of privilege.
thread.changed: The clash moved from the Lok Sabha to the Rajya Sabha, where Congress's Pramod Tiwari cited Article 75 to demand Shah personally answer, and Gandhi publicly asked why Shah is 'scared' to face Parliament.

stories.title: Tajinderpal Singh Toor qualifies for the Commonwealth Games shot put final, setting up a duel with defending champion Tom Walsh
key_points: India's shot put national record holder **Tajinderpal Singh Toor** threw **20.14m** to qualify for Thursday's final.
New Zealand's **Tom Walsh**, the defending Commonwealth Games champion, topped qualifying with a first-round **21.03m**.
Fellow Indian **Samardeep Singh Gill** also advanced to the final.
Toor is chasing his **first-ever Commonwealth Games medal** in the event.
The final takes place **Friday, July 31**.
stories.background: **Tajinderpal Singh Toor** holds the Indian national record in shot put and has been one of India's most consistent throwers for years, but a Commonwealth Games medal in the event has eluded him so far. **Tom Walsh** of New Zealand is the reigning Commonwealth Games champion and one of the most dominant shot putters in the world, making him the clear favorite heading into Friday's final.
stories.what_happened: In Wednesday's qualifying round at the **2026 Commonwealth Games** in Glasgow, Toor sealed his spot in the final with a **20.14m** throw on his second attempt, finishing second overall behind Walsh's opening throw of **21.03m**. Fellow Indian competitor Samardeep Singh Gill also progressed through qualifying. Both will now compete in Friday's medal final against Walsh and the rest of the qualified field.
stories.why_it_matters: A shot put medal would be a breakthrough for Toor, who has long been talked about as one of India's best field-event prospects without a Commonwealth Games podium finish to show for it.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong Indian showing in the shot put final adds to the country's field-event medal push in Glasgow, alongside javelin and long jump, and raises Toor's profile heading into future global meets.
stories.why_now: Qualifying concluded Wednesday, setting the field for Friday's final at the ongoing Commonwealth Games.
stories.watch_next: The men's shot put final on Friday, July 31, where Toor faces defending champion Tom Walsh.
stories.the_lesson: In throwing events, qualifying position doesn't decide medals — Toor goes into the final needing to beat, not just match, the best throw of the day to have a real shot at gold.

stories.title: Bangladesh strips Mehidy Hasan Miraz of the ODI captaincy, hands the reins to Litton Das
key_points: The **Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB)** named **Litton Das** as the new ODI captain, replacing **Mehidy Hasan Miraz**.
Litton already led the **T20I** side and now captains Bangladesh in **both** white-ball formats.
**Towhid Hridoy** becomes ODI vice-captain; **Najmul Hossain Shanto** stays on as **Test** captain.
The change follows a **2-1 ODI series loss to Zimbabwe** earlier this month under Miraz's leadership.
Miraz, **31**, had captained the ODI side only since **June 2025**.
stories.background: Bangladesh has increasingly split captaincy duties across its three formats — Test, ODI, and T20I — rather than relying on one all-format leader, a model several major cricket boards have adopted as the international calendar gets busier. Mehidy Hasan Miraz had held the ODI captaincy since June 2025, but Bangladesh's form in the 50-over format has been shaky, including a recent series defeat to Zimbabwe, a team they'd typically be expected to beat.
stories.what_happened: BCB president Tamim Iqbal announced after a board meeting in Mirpur that Litton Das, who already captains Bangladesh's T20I side, will now also lead the ODI team, taking over from Mehidy Hasan Miraz. Towhid Hridoy was named ODI vice-captain. Najmul Hossain Shanto continues as Test captain, so Bangladesh's three formats now have two captains between them rather than three. Tamim explained the board's logic as twofold: rewarding Litton's leadership qualities, and freeing up Miraz to focus purely on playing rather than captaincy duties, after Bangladesh's 2-1 ODI series loss to Zimbabwe this month.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a significant leadership shake-up for a national team heading toward the 2027 ODI World Cup, with the board explicitly citing the need to fix the 50-over side's form well ahead of that tournament.
stories.ripple_effects: Miraz's role shifts to senior-player-without-captaincy-burden, which teams often use to extend a strong player's career; Litton now carries the weight of two formats' leadership simultaneously, a workload that has strained other players in the past. It also puts pressure on Bangladesh's next ODI assignments to show quick results, or the new setup will face scrutiny fast.
stories.why_now: The change follows directly from this month's ODI series loss to Zimbabwe, which the board treated as the trigger to act ahead of the next international window.
stories.watch_next: Watch Bangladesh's next ODI series for early signs of whether the captaincy change lifts results, and whether Litton is given a longer runway than Miraz's roughly one-year tenure.
stories.the_lesson: Sports boards often use a leadership change as the lowest-cost way to signal accountability for poor results, even when the deeper causes — squad depth, form, conditions — may have little to do with who's captain.

stories.title: Pakistan's Shan Masood ruled out of the second West Indies Test with a fractured finger

thread.previously: We reported West Indies beat Pakistan by 90 runs in the first Test, Pakistan's fourth consecutive Test defeat under Babar Azam's captaincy.
thread.changed: It has now emerged that senior batter **Shan Masood fractured a finger during that same first Test** and will miss the second and final Test starting August 2, with Babar Azam continuing as captain.

key_points: Shan Masood **fractured the index finger on his left hand** after being struck by a delivery from West Indies fast bowler **Jayden Seales**.
The injury happened on the **third day of the first Test**, which Pakistan went on to lose by 90 runs.
Masood will **miss the second and final Test**, which starts August 2 at Queen's Park Oval in Trinidad.
**Babar Azam continues as Pakistan's Test captain**, a role he already held for this series.
Pakistan's team management is now weighing **Abdullah Shafique or Saud Shakeel** as Masood's batting replacement.
stories.background: Shan Masood is a senior Pakistan Test batter and a former captain of the side, though Babar Azam has been leading the Test team for this tour. Pakistan arrived in the West Indies already under pressure after a run of poor Test results, and the first Test loss extended that run to four straight defeats. Fast bowler Jayden Seales has been among the more dangerous quicks for West Indies in this series.
stories.what_happened: During the third day of the first Test against West Indies, Shan Masood was struck on his left hand by a delivery from fast bowler Jayden Seales, fracturing his index finger. Pakistan went on to lose that Test by 90 runs, their fourth consecutive Test defeat. The injury has now ruled Masood out of the second and final Test, which begins **August 2 at Queen's Park Oval** in Trinidad, with the series already 1-0 in West Indies' favour. Babar Azam, who was already captaining the side for this series, will continue in that role, while Pakistan's team management decides between **Abdullah Shafique and Saud Shakeel** to replace Masood in the batting order.
stories.why_it_matters: Losing a senior batter to injury while already 1-0 down and on a four-match losing streak deepens the pressure on a Pakistan Test side already searching for form and consistency.
stories.ripple_effects: Whoever replaces Masood gets a high-stakes opportunity to cement a middle-order spot ahead of Pakistan's home Test series against England starting August 19, making this a de facto audition.
stories.why_now: The finger fracture and its knock-on effect on team selection were only confirmed this week, ahead of the second Test starting August 2.
stories.watch_next: Watch Pakistan's playing XI announcement for the second Test to see who replaces Masood in the batting order.
stories.the_lesson: A single injury during a losing effort can compound a team's problems well beyond that match — the fallout (a forced reshuffle, an audition under pressure) often plays out over the following games, not just the one where it happened.

stories.title: Hardik Pandya's IPL trade saga turns into a bidding war as CSK counters with Brevis, KKR and RR jump in

thread.previously: We reported CSK had re-emerged as the front-runner to acquire Hardik Pandya from Mumbai Indians, with the trade saga still dragging on unresolved.
thread.changed: Mumbai Indians' initial demand of Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre from CSK has been rejected; **CSK is countering with Dube, Dewald Brevis, and roughly ₹10 crore in cash instead**, while up to **seven IPL franchises — including KKR and RR — have now entered the race** for Pandya.

key_points: Mumbai Indians initially wanted **Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre** from CSK in exchange for captain Hardik Pandya.
CSK refused to include Mhatre and instead countered with **Dube, Dewald Brevis, and roughly ₹10 crore in cash**.
As many as **seven IPL franchises**, including Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals, have now shown interest in signing Pandya.
Pandya's trade value has taken a hit after a **modest IPL 2026 season**: just 206 runs at an average of 22.89, with no half-centuries.
KKR is being described as a serious fallback destination if the **CSK-Mumbai swap talks collapse**.
stories.background: Hardik Pandya has captained Mumbai Indians since a high-profile trade brought him back to the franchise, but MI's underwhelming recent form and Pandya's own dip in batting output have put his future with the team in question. IPL teams can trade contracted players between seasons in negotiated deals, often involving a mix of players and cash, and Pandya — as a former captain with a marquee name — has become one of this off-season's biggest trade chips.
stories.what_happened: Mumbai Indians opened trade talks with Chennai Super Kings by asking for young all-rounder Shivam Dube and rising batter Ayush Mhatre in exchange for Hardik Pandya. **CSK refused to part with Mhatre**, instead offering a counter-package of Dube, South African batter Dewald Brevis, and roughly ₹10 crore in cash. While that negotiation continues, the situation has escalated into a genuine bidding war: reports now say as many as **seven IPL franchises**, including Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals, have expressed interest in acquiring Pandya if the Mumbai-Chennai deal falls through. Adding pressure to the situation, Pandya's IPL 2026 season was modest by his standards — just 206 runs at an average of 22.89 and a strike rate of 138.26, with no half-centuries, a form dip that may be affecting how much other teams are willing to offer for him.
stories.why_it_matters: A captain of Pandya's profile being fought over by seven franchises shows how aggressively IPL teams are willing to restructure their squads mid-cycle when a marquee player's form dips — trade windows are increasingly being used like a mini-auction.
stories.ripple_effects: Wherever Pandya lands will reshape that franchise's captaincy plans and bowling attack for the next IPL season, while Mumbai Indians will need to rebuild their leadership structure if the trade goes through.
stories.why_now: This is a live, ongoing negotiation entering a more competitive phase this week as rival franchises formally enter the race.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether CSK's counter-offer of Dube, Brevis and cash is accepted, or whether Pandya ends up at KKR or RR instead.

key_terms.definition: A period between IPL seasons when franchises can negotiate to swap contracted players, often with cash included, outside of the annual auction.

stories.the_lesson: In any market with fixed rosters and a trade deadline, a star performer's price is set as much by team need and leverage as by their raw stats — a modest season can still trigger a bidding war if enough teams need what that player still offers.

stories.title: Shubman Gill reclaims the No. 1 spot in ICC's ODI batting rankings
key_points: Gill returned to **No. 1** in the ICC ODI batting rankings, his **third spell** at the top.
He overtook New Zealand's **Daryl Mitchell**, who dropped from the top spot after being ruled out of a Bridgetown ODI with a hip strain.
Gill's rise follows a strong run against England, where he scored **188 runs in 3 matches**.
He now has **3,379 runs in 67 ODIs**, including **9 centuries** and **20 half-centuries**.
Gill captains both India's ODI and Test sides, adding weight to his status as the team's batting anchor across formats.
stories.background: The ICC batting rankings are a running points system based on recent performances, weighted more heavily toward matches against strong opposition and in bigger tournaments. Shubman Gill has held the ODI No. 1 spot before, but lost it earlier this year as other batters, including New Zealand's Daryl Mitchell, went on stronger streaks. Gill was named India's ODI and Test captain in 2026, putting extra scrutiny on his own batting form as he leads both sides.
stories.what_happened: Shubman Gill reclaimed the No. 1 ranking among ODI batters after a strong showing in India's recently concluded series against England, where he scored 188 runs across three matches. He leapfrogged New Zealand's Daryl Mitchell, who had held the top spot since January but slipped after being ruled out of the final ODI against West Indies in Bridgetown with a low-grade hip strain. This marks Gill's third stint at the top of the ODI rankings, and comes with his career tally now at 3,379 runs in 67 ODIs, including 9 centuries and 20 half-centuries.
stories.why_it_matters: As India's ODI and Test captain, Gill's batting form is directly tied to the team's results and confidence heading into major tournaments — a captain who is also the world's top-ranked batter in a format strengthens both his authority and India's title chances.
stories.ripple_effects: A red-hot captain at the top of the rankings raises expectations for India's ODI side heading toward the next 50-over World Cup cycle, and adds to selectors' confidence in Gill's leadership across formats.
stories.why_now: The ranking update reflects Gill's performances in India's just-finished ODI series against England, combined with Daryl Mitchell's injury-enforced absence from New Zealand's Bridgetown ODI.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether Gill can hold the No. 1 spot through India's upcoming Sri Lanka Test series and any ODI assignments later in the year.
stories.the_lesson: Rankings in sport are relative, not absolute — Gill's return to No. 1 came from a mix of his own strong form and a rival's misfortune, a reminder that being "best in the world" often depends on who else stumbles.

stories.title: ICC confirms 12 venues across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia for the 2027 World Cup
key_points: The ICC has confirmed **12 host venues** for the 2027 Men's Cricket World Cup.
Matches will be split across **South Africa (8 venues), Zimbabwe (3) and Namibia (1)**.
It's a **50-over tournament** featuring **14 teams and 57 matches**.
The World Cup returns to **Africa for the first time in 24 years**.
The venues and tournament brand were revealed at a **launch event in Johannesburg**.
stories.background: The Cricket World Cup is the sport's flagship 50-over (One Day International) tournament, held roughly every four years. Africa last hosted the men's World Cup in 2003 (South Africa, Zimbabwe and Kenya), so this 2027 edition marks a long-awaited return of the tournament to the continent. Confirming host venues years in advance lets host boards plan stadium upgrades, ticketing, and broadcast infrastructure, and gives fans and travelling teams a clear roadmap.
stories.what_happened: The ICC officially unveiled the 12 venues for the 2027 Men's Cricket World Cup at a launch event in Johannesburg. South Africa will host the bulk of matches across 8 grounds — Wanderers Stadium (Johannesburg), SuperSport Park (Centurion), Newlands (Cape Town), Kingsmead (Durban), St George's Park (Gqeberha), Mangaung Oval (Bloemfontein), Boland Park (Paarl) and Buffalo Park (KuGompo City, formerly East London). Zimbabwe will host games at Harare Sports Club, Queens Sports Club (Bulawayo) and the Victoria Falls stadium. Namibia's Windhoek ground will also host matches. The tournament will run as a 50-over competition with 14 teams playing 57 matches in total.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a big moment for African cricket — hosting rights bring investment, infrastructure upgrades, and a global spotlight to a region that hasn't had the men's World Cup in over two decades.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect a wave of stadium renovation and ticketing news from South African, Zimbabwean and Namibian cricket boards over the next year, plus qualification-path stories as teams jostle for the 14 World Cup spots.
stories.why_now: The ICC confirmed the venues today at a dedicated launch ceremony, more than a year ahead of the tournament.
stories.watch_next: The release of the full match schedule and qualification pathway for the remaining World Cup spots.
stories.the_lesson: Major global sporting events are announced years ahead of time because hosting infrastructure — stadiums, transport, broadcast — takes that long to prepare properly.

stories.title: Stephen Fleming named England's new Test coach as Joe Root returns as captain
key_points: The **ECB** has named former New Zealand captain **Stephen Fleming** as England's new men's Test head coach.
**Joe Root** returns as Test captain, a role he left back in **2022**.
Fleming replaces **Brendon McCullum**, who was sacked in June after poor results and off-field issues.
Fleming signed a **four-year deal running through September 2030**.
He won't start immediately — **Marcus Trescothick** is interim coach until after the Pakistan series begins.
stories.background: England's Test team has been going through turbulence: head coach Brendon McCullum, who oversaw the aggressive 'Bazball' era, was sacked in June 2026 following a run of poor results and off-field incidents. Stephen Fleming is one of the most respected figures in world cricket — New Zealand's most successful Test captain across 111 matches, and more recently the long-serving, highly rated head coach of Chennai Super Kings in the IPL for 18 years, a role he only just left. Joe Root previously captained England's Test side until 2022, when he stepped down and Ben Stokes took over — Root staying on as the team's best batter throughout.
stories.what_happened: The England and Wales Cricket Board announced Stephen Fleming, 52, as the new England men's Test head coach — his first job leading a national team, after an 18-year association with Chennai Super Kings in the IPL. He replaces Brendon McCullum, sacked in June. Fleming has signed a four-year deal that runs until the end of September 2030. Alongside the coaching change, **Joe Root has been reappointed England Test captain**, returning to a role he left in 2022. Fleming will not take over immediately — he'll start after England's series against Pakistan begins, with Marcus Trescothick serving as interim head coach in the meantime.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a major changing of the guard for one of cricket's most prominent Test teams — a new coaching philosophy from a widely respected coach, combined with Root's return to leadership, could reshape England's approach after the McCullum era.
stories.ripple_effects: It affects England's tactics, team selection, and captaincy dynamics with Ben Stokes (the current all-format leader) heading into a busy international calendar; it also closes the door on Fleming links to other vacant coaching jobs speculated about elsewhere in the sport.
stories.why_now: The appointment was formally confirmed today by the ECB, ending weeks of speculation about who would replace McCullum.
stories.watch_next: How the England dressing room dynamic looks once Fleming formally takes over after the Pakistan series begins.

key_terms.definition: The head coach specifically responsible for a national team's 5-day format (Test cricket), as opposed to white-ball formats which can have separate coaching setups.

stories.the_lesson: Leadership changes in sport are rarely just about one person — they ripple into captaincy, tactics, and team culture all at once.

stories.title: India names its Sri Lanka Test squad around Bumrah's fitness test, with a shock call-up for uncapped all-rounder Saransh Jain

thread.previously: We reported that Jasprit Bumrah's BCCI-mandated rest period was ending today, July 30, after which he would report to the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru for his next fitness check.
thread.changed: BCCI has now named the full 15-man Test squad for the Sri Lanka tour built around that timeline — Bumrah and Sai Sudharsan are included but only subject to passing that fitness clearance, Ravindra Jadeja returns from a tennis-elbow injury, and uncapped all-rounder Saransh Jain gets a shock maiden call-up after Washington Sundar was ruled out hurt.

key_points: **Jasprit Bumrah** and **Sai Sudharsan** are in the 15-man squad, but only if they clear a fitness test at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence.
**Ravindra Jadeja** returns after recovering from a tennis-elbow injury that had ruled him out.
**Saransh Jain**, a 33-year-old Madhya Pradesh spin-bowling all-rounder, earns a **maiden Test call-up**.
Jain's selection came after **Washington Sundar** was ruled out with a hamstring injury from the England ODIs.
**Shubman Gill** continues as captain, with **KL Rahul** as vice-captain, for the two-Test series starting **August 15**.
stories.background: India's fast-bowling spearhead **Jasprit Bumrah** has been carefully managed through 2026 to protect his fitness, missing white-ball assignments and the Champions Trophy earlier this year, and playing Test cricket only since last year's T20 World Cup final. The BCCI had scheduled his rest to end on **July 30**, after which he would report to the **Centre of Excellence (CoE)** in Bengaluru — the board's dedicated fitness and rehab facility — for the medical clearance that decides whether he actually plays. India also needed to replace the injured **Washington Sundar**, opening a spot that went to a surprise, uncapped domestic performer.
stories.what_happened: The BCCI on **July 28** announced its 15-member squad for a two-Test series in **Sri Lanka**, beginning **August 15**, after a four-day practice match in Colombo from August 7. **Jasprit Bumrah** and top-order batter **Sai Sudharsan** are both named, but selectors made their inclusion conditional on clearing a fitness test at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence — Bumrah's rest period was set to end exactly on **July 30**, the day he was due to report there. **Ravindra Jadeja** returns to the squad after recovering from tennis elbow. **Saransh Jain**, a 33-year-old off-spinning all-rounder from Madhya Pradesh who has never played for India, received a **maiden call-up** after Washington Sundar was ruled out with a hamstring injury sustained during the England ODIs. **Shubman Gill** continues as captain and **KL Rahul** as vice-captain.
stories.why_it_matters: Whether Bumrah — India's most important bowler — actually plays the series hinges entirely on a fitness test happening right around now, making today's medical check the real decision point behind a squad that was already announced two days ago.
stories.ripple_effects: If Bumrah or Sudharsan fail their fitness tests, India would need to call up a replacement on short notice before the practice match in Colombo starting August 7, potentially reshaping the bowling attack for a series that also doubles as preparation for future assignments. Saransh Jain's call-up, at 33, also highlights how India's selectors are willing to reward uncapped domestic performers over more famous names when injuries strike.
stories.why_now: Today, July 30, is the exact date Bumrah's BCCI-mandated rest period was scheduled to end and he was due to report to the Centre of Excellence — the fitness check that will determine whether the squad named two days ago actually takes the field as announced.
stories.watch_next: Watch for confirmation of Bumrah's and Sai Sudharsan's fitness test results, and any replacement call-ups before the Colombo practice match starting August 7.

key_terms.definition: The BCCI's dedicated training and rehabilitation facility in Bengaluru, where injured or rested players are cleared to return to the national team.

stories.the_lesson: A squad announcement isn't always the final word — when key players are picked 'subject to fitness,' the real decision happens later, at a medical test, not at the press conference.

stories.title: Shane McDermott quits Pakistan's coaching staff to become Afghanistan's fielding coach
key_points: The **Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB)** confirmed Shane McDermott as its new **assistant and fielding coach** on July 29, 2026.
McDermott **resigned from the Pakistan Cricket Board** on July 18, after a year in the same fielding-coach role there.
He previously worked with **Afghanistan from January 2024 to July 2025**, before his stint with Pakistan.
He is set to **join the Afghanistan squad on August 1**, ahead of a **five-match ODI series against Ireland**.
The move is a rare case of a coach switching directly **between two rival national teams** within the same year.
stories.background: International cricket coaching staff — batting, bowling, and fielding coaches — frequently move between national teams, but doing so between two sides that regularly play each other, like Afghanistan and Pakistan, is unusual and can draw scrutiny over potential conflicts of interest, since the coach knows a rival team's methods and personnel intimately. Fielding coaches specifically work on catching, ground fielding, and athleticism — an area increasingly seen as a difference-maker in modern limited-overs cricket.
stories.what_happened: The **Afghanistan Cricket Board officially confirmed** on July 29, 2026 that Shane McDermott has been appointed the national team's new **Assistant and Fielding Coach**. McDermott previously held the same fielding-coach role with Afghanistan from **January 2024 to July 2025**, before moving to a similar position with the **Pakistan Cricket Board from July 2025**. He resigned from the Pakistan role on **July 18, 2026**, roughly eighteen days before his new Afghanistan appointment was confirmed. McDermott is scheduled to formally **join Afghanistan's coaching staff on August 1, 2026**, in time to prepare the team for its upcoming **five-match ODI series against Ireland**.
stories.why_it_matters: Fielding standards have become a genuine competitive differentiator in modern white-ball cricket, and a coach who knows Pakistan's methods intimately now works for one of its regional rivals — a small but real edge for Afghanistan, and a talking point about coaching-market movement between competing cricket boards.
stories.ripple_effects: Afghanistan gets an experienced fielding coach with recent, direct knowledge of a key rival team just as it heads into a big ODI series — potentially sharpening Afghanistan's fielding standards quickly, given McDermott already has a working relationship with several of the squad's senior players from his earlier stint.
stories.why_now: The appointment is surfacing today because the ACB's confirmation came July 29, 2026, with McDermott's formal start date just days away on August 1.
stories.watch_next: Watch Afghanistan's fielding performance in the opening ODI of the Ireland series for an early read on McDermott's impact.
stories.the_lesson: Specialist expertise — like fielding coaching — increasingly moves across boundaries and rivalries in professional sport, because the value of the skill outweighs old loyalties.

stories.title: England captain Nat Sciver-Brunt targets a return to bowling — but may sit out the Ireland ODIs
key_points: Sciver-Brunt says she **doesn't want to give up bowling** despite a recurring calf injury, targeting an all-rounder comeback.
She suffered the injury during **The Hundred**, England's domestic short-format tournament, earlier this month.
She has **hinted she may miss** England's ODI series against Ireland next month to protect her recovery.
Her rehab is being **carefully managed** by England's medical and performance staff to avoid a repeat injury.
As **England Women's captain**, her fitness directly affects the team's balance ahead of a busy international calendar.
stories.background: **Nat Sciver-Brunt** is England Women's captain and one of the team's most important all-rounders, meaning she contributes as both a top-order batter and a bowler, giving England extra tactical flexibility. Losing her bowling contribution, even temporarily, forces England to rebalance its bowling attack and batting order. She picked up a calf injury — a strain in the lower leg muscle — while playing in **The Hundred**, England's short, fast domestic cricket competition that runs through the English summer.
stories.what_happened: Nat Sciver-Brunt said in comments published July 30, 2026 that she is determined to return to bowling as soon as her recovery allows, stating 'I don't want to give up the bowling just yet,' after sustaining a **calf injury** during The Hundred earlier this month. She confirmed she is currently focused on rehabilitation and that her return is being carefully staged by England's medical and performance staff specifically to avoid the injury recurring. Sciver-Brunt has **hinted she could miss England's ODI series against Ireland next month** in order to prioritise a full recovery over rushing back for a lower-stakes series, with her sights instead set on being fully fit for bigger assignments later in the international calendar.
stories.why_it_matters: As captain and a genuine all-rounder, Sciver-Brunt's fitness is a significant factor in England Women's team balance — her absence changes both the batting order and bowling options, and any recurring calf issue raises longer-term fitness-management questions ahead of the team's biggest upcoming series.
stories.ripple_effects: If she does sit out the Ireland series, England will need to test alternative bowling and batting-order combinations without their captain, giving other players a chance to step up and giving team management valuable data on squad depth ahead of bigger tournaments.
stories.why_now: Her comments came today, July 30, 2026, as she updates fans and media on her recovery timeline ahead of squad selection for the Ireland series.
stories.watch_next: Watch for England's official squad announcement for the Ireland ODI series to see whether Sciver-Brunt is included.

key_terms.definition: A cricket player skilled at both batting and bowling, giving their team extra flexibility in team selection and tactics.

stories.the_lesson: In sport, protecting a slow, proper recovery from a recurring injury is often the higher-value long-term decision, even when it means missing a nearer-term match.

stories.title: Stephen Fleming set to become England's new Test coach, replacing Brendon McCullum
key_points: Former **New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming** has emerged as the clear frontrunner to become England's new **Test head coach**.
The **ECB (England and Wales Cricket Board)** is reportedly close to confirming Fleming's appointment after a round of interviews concluded this week.
Fleming, 53, would replace fellow Kiwi **Brendon McCullum**, who is leaving the Test role.

He beat out competition including English coaches **Richard Dawson and Jonathan Trott**, and Australian **Tom Moody**; early favorite **Andy Flower** withdrew to focus on his franchise coaching roles.

The ECB is expected to let assistant coach **Marcus Trescothick** lead the team on an **interim basis** for the upcoming Pakistan series, with Fleming taking full charge for the **December tour of South Africa**.
stories.background: Brendon McCullum has coached England's Test team since 2022, helping popularize the aggressive 'Bazball' approach to Test cricket that transformed the team's results and style of play. Stephen Fleming, one of New Zealand's most respected former captains with **111 Test caps**, has built a second career as a hugely successful franchise coach — he has won **five IPL titles with Chennai Super Kings** and has also coached CSK's sister franchises in South Africa's SA20 and the US's Major League Cricket. He also has roots in English cricket, having played for Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire and coached Southern Brave in England's Hundred competition.
stories.what_happened: **Stephen Fleming has emerged as the favourite to become England's new Test head coach**, with the ECB reportedly close to finalizing his appointment after interviews wrapped up this week. He is set to **replace Brendon McCullum**, who is stepping away from the Test coaching role. Fleming saw off competition from English coaches Richard Dawson and Jonathan Trott and Australia's Tom Moody, while earlier favourite **Andy Flower withdrew** from consideration to concentrate on his existing franchise commitments with Royal Challengers Bengaluru and London Spirit. Because Fleming has ongoing IPL and franchise obligations, the ECB is expected to have **assistant coach Marcus Trescothick take interim charge** of the team for the upcoming **Test series against Pakistan**, with Fleming stepping in to lead the side fully for **December's tour of South Africa**.
stories.why_it_matters: England's Test coaching job is one of the most scrutinized roles in world cricket, and this appointment marks the end of the high-profile, high-scoring 'Bazball' era under McCullum. Fleming's franchise-honed coaching style and calm reputation would mark a real change in tone for a team known lately for aggression and risk-taking.
stories.ripple_effects: Fleming's move creates a coaching vacancy question at Chennai Super Kings and his other franchise sides, and gives England's players an interim adjustment period under Trescothick before their new permanent coach fully arrives. It could also reshape England's tactical approach heading into major series against Pakistan and South Africa.
stories.why_now: The ECB's coaching search concluded its interview round this week, with reports of Fleming's frontrunner status and the interim Trescothick plan surfacing together as the decision neared.
stories.watch_next: Official confirmation of Fleming's appointment by the ECB, and how Trescothick's England side performs in the interim Pakistan Test series starting August 19 at Headingley.
stories.the_lesson: In cricket coaching, franchise success increasingly counts as much as international playing pedigree when national boards choose a head coach — it's now a genuinely global coaching marketplace.
